summary.text: The block \((2,4,2,4,2)\) would require primes at offsets \(0,2,6,8,12,14\) from some starting prime; reducing these six numbers modulo \(5\) forces one to equal \(5\), with the only apparent alternative producing the composite number \(9\). Hence the block occurs only once, starting with the prime \(5\), so it cannot recur infinitely often.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
P_1=2,
 P_2=3,
 P_3=5,
 P_4=7,
 P_5=11,
 P_6=13,
 P_7=17,
 P_8=19,
\ldots
\]
denote the primes in strictly increasing order. Thus the OEIS sequence is
\[
a(n)=P_{n+1}-P_n \qquad (n\ge 1).
\]
If, as in the formal statement, the sequence is also assigned a value at index zero, that value is defined to be \(a(0)=0\). This harmless extension will be dealt with explicitly below.

We disprove the assertion by considering the admissible starting index \(n=3>2\) and taking \(m=4\), so that the relevant block has five terms. From the displayed list of primes,
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(3)&=P_4-P_3=7-5=2,\\
a(4)&=P_5-P_4=11-7=4,\\
a(5)&=P_6-P_5=13-11=2,\\
a(6)&=P_7-P_6=17-13=4,\\
a(7)&=P_8-P_7=19-17=2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Consequently the block beginning at index \(3\) is
\[
(a(3),a(4),a(5),a(6),a(7))=(2,4,2,4,2).
\]
We will prove that this block occurs nowhere else.

Suppose that for some index \(k\) one has
\[
(a(k),a(k+1),a(k+2),a(k+3),a(k+4))=(2,4,2,4,2). \tag{1}
\]
The extended index \(k=0\) is impossible, since then the first entry would be \(a(0)=0\), whereas the first entry in (1) is \(2\). Hence \(k\ge 1\), and we may set
\[
q=P_k.
\]
In particular, \(q\) is prime.

Starting with \(P_k=q\) and successively adding the five gaps in (1), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
P_{k+1}&=q+2,\\
P_{k+2}&=(q+2)+4=q+6,\\
P_{k+3}&=(q+6)+2=q+8,\\
P_{k+4}&=(q+8)+4=q+12,\\
P_{k+5}&=(q+12)+2=q+14.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus all six numbers
\[
q,
 q+2,
 q+6,
 q+8,
 q+12,
 q+14 \tag{2}
\]
are prime. Their being consecutive primes is part of how they arose, but for the modular obstruction below we only need their primality.

We use the elementary fact that if a prime number \(r\) is divisible by \(5\), then \(r=5\). Indeed, because \(5\mid r\) and \(r\) is prime, the positive divisor \(5\) of \(r\) must be either \(1\) or \(r\); it is not \(1\), so it equals \(r\).

Now consider the five possible residues of \(q\) modulo \(5\).

1. If \(q\equiv 0\pmod 5\), then \(q\) itself is a prime divisible by \(5\), so the preceding fact gives
\[
q=5. \tag{3}
\]

2. If \(q\equiv 1\pmod 5\), then
\[
q+14\equiv 1+14\equiv 0\pmod 5.
\]
The number \(q+14\) is prime by (2), so it would have to equal \(5\). This is impossible: since \(q\) is a positive prime, \(q+14>5\).

3. If \(q\equiv 2\pmod 5\), then
\[
q+8\equiv 2+8\equiv 0\pmod 5.
\]
Again, \(q+8\) is prime by (2), and hence would have to equal \(5\), which is impossible because \(q+8>5\).

4. If \(q\equiv 3\pmod 5\), then
\[
q+2\equiv 3+2\equiv 0\pmod 5.
\]
Since \(q+2\) is prime, this forces \(q+2=5\), and therefore \(q=3\). But then another member of (2) is
\[
q+6=3+6=9,
\]
which is not prime because \(9=3\cdot 3\). This contradicts the primality of \(q+6=P_{k+2}\).

5. Finally, if \(q\equiv 4\pmod 5\), then
\[
q+6\equiv 4+6\equiv 0\pmod 5.
\]
The prime \(q+6\) would therefore have to equal \(5\), again impossible because \(q+6>5\).

These five cases are exhaustive. Four lead to contradictions, while the residue-zero case gives \(q=5\). Therefore every occurrence of the block (1) must begin with the prime
\[
P_k=q=5.
\]

a is the third prime: \(P_3=5\). Since the sequence of primes is strictly increasing, no prime can appear at two different indices. Hence \(P_k=P_3\) implies
\[
k=3.
\]
Thus the five-term block \((2,4,2,4,2)\) occurs exactly once, at starting index \(3\). It does occur there by the initial direct calculation, and the argument above proves that no other starting index is possible. Therefore
\[
\{k:(a(k),a(k+1),a(k+2),a(k+3),a(k+4))
=(a(3),a(4),a(5),a(6),a(7))\}=\{3\},
\]
a finite singleton.

The conjecture claims that for every \(n>2\) and every \(m\ge 0\), the block
\[
a(n),\ldots,a(n+m)
\]
has infinitely many starting indices at which it reappears. Taking \(n=3\) and \(m=4\) yields the block just analyzed, whose set of occurrences is the singleton \(\{3\}\), not an infinite set. This contradicts the asserted universal statement and therefore disproves the conjecture.
